Pompey

Biography

Pompey

Enslaved Freedom Fighter of Exuma · Bahamian National Hero · Leader of the 1830 Revolt

The World That Made a Hero

To understand Pompey — the man, the rebel, the legend — one must first understand the world that forged him: the sun-scorched cotton estates of Exuma, The Bahamas, a world constructed entirely upon the exploitation of enslaved African men and women, and the audacious, violent machinery of empire that sustained it.

The Bahamas had not always been an agricultural colony. The island chain's poor, thin soils and fickle rains made large-scale plantation farming a marginal enterprise. But history changed course dramatically after the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783), when thousands of Loyalist settlers — planters and merchants who had remained loyal to the British Crown — fled the newly independent United States and sought refuge in the British Caribbean. The British government offered generous land grants across the Bahamian islands to compensate these displaced settlers, and with the Loyalists came their most valuable and most brutalized asset: enslaved African people.

Among the most prominent of these Loyalist landowners was Denys Rolle (1725–1797), a wealthy British landowner who had earlier attempted to establish a utopian agricultural settlement called Rollestown in East Florida. When Britain ceded Florida to Spain following the Revolutionary War, Denys Rolle relocated his entire enslaved workforce — men, women, and children — to approximately 7,000 acres of land he was granted on Great Exuma in the Bahamas. On this land, the enslaved workers cleared bush, built homes, cultivated provision grounds, and established the plantation settlements that would become known as Steventon, Rolleville, and Rolle Town.

When Denys Rolle died in 1797, his son, Lord John Rolle (1750–1842), inherited the Exuma estates. Unlike his father, Lord John Rolle resided primarily in England as an absentee landlord, managing his Bahamian holdings through an overseer. The distance between owner and plantation deepened the cruelties of the system — overseers had enormous power over the lives of the enslaved, and conditions on the Rolle estates became notoriously brutal. By the eve of emancipation, Lord Rolle held somewhere between 350 and 400 enslaved people, making him one of the single largest slaveholders in the entire Bahamas.

It was into this world — a world of forced labor, broken families, and systematic dehumanization — that Pompey was born, likely around 1798, on the Rolle plantation in Steventon, Great Exuma.

Who Was Pompey?

Almost nothing of Pompey's personal history was recorded by those who held power over him. Enslaved people in the British Caribbean were catalogued in plantation ledgers not as individuals with histories, hopes, and families, but as units of labor and property — counted alongside livestock and tools. What we know of Pompey comes primarily from colonial administrative records surrounding the 1830 rebellion he led, and from the oral traditions preserved by the Exumian community across generations.

What the historical record does tell us is this: by 1830, Pompey was approximately 32 years old, a blacksmith by trade, and a recognized leader within the enslaved community of the Rolle Plantation. A blacksmith in the plantation hierarchy occupied a position of relative skill and visibility — forging and repairing the iron tools that made agricultural work possible, Pompey would have moved between the fields, the forge, and the plantation quarters. He would have known nearly everyone on the estate. He would have understood, with particular clarity, how the machinery of slavery worked — and perhaps, how it might be broken.

There is no evidence that Pompey ever personally met Lord Rolle, who remained comfortably in England while the suffering on his estates deepened. But the actions Pompey took in 1830 would reverberate all the way to the colonial government in Nassau, and far beyond.

The Crisis of 1830: Relocation and Resistance

By the late 1820s, the soil of the Rolle estates in Exuma had been largely exhausted by decades of intensive cotton cultivation. The agricultural model that the Loyalists had imported from the American South was failing across the Bahamas — the thin limestone soils of the out-islands simply could not sustain the punishing demands of cash-crop agriculture indefinitely. To maximize profit on his remaining fertile holdings, Lord Rolle's overseer announced in 1829–1830 a sweeping plan: 77 enslaved men, women, and children from the Steventon plantation were to be forcibly relocated to Cat Island, where the land remained more productive.

For the enslaved community of Steventon, this decree was nothing short of catastrophic. They had spent decades — indeed, generations — building lives on this land. They had cultivated provision grounds where they grew their own food. They had established kinship networks, friendships, family structures, and community ties that gave meaning and dignity to lives otherwise defined by bondage. To be moved like livestock to another island, to have everything familiar ripped away with no recourse, no appeal, no voice — this was an act of profound violence, even within the brutal logic of the slave system itself.

Pompey refused to accept it.

"He accepted thirty-nine lashes of the whip rather than see his people moved against their will — and in doing so, he told the world that these people were not property. They were human beings with the right to remain where they had built their homes."

In an act of organized, strategic defiance, Pompey led a group of approximately 44 to 80 enslaved people into the bush of Great Exuma, evading their overseers and refusing to board the transport vessel that would carry them to Cat Island. For several weeks, they hid among the scrub forests and cays of the island, beyond the reach of plantation authority. But Pompey's ambitions went far beyond simple flight.

The Voyage to Nassau: A 130-Mile Act of Courage

Rather than merely escaping into the bush, Pompey organized something far bolder. The group seized one of Lord Rolle's own boats and set sail for Nassau — the capital of the Bahamas, some 130 miles away — with the explicit intention of petitioning the British Governor directly to halt their forced relocation.

This was an extraordinary act, remarkable for both its audacity and its strategic sophistication. Pompey and his companions were not simply running away from slavery. They were attempting to use the legal and political structures of the colonial system against the plantation class — appealing to British imperial authority, which, by 1830, was increasingly sympathetic to abolitionist sentiment, to protect their rights as human beings.

The group was intercepted before reaching Nassau and returned to Exuma under armed escort. But the damage to planter authority had already been done. The news of their bold voyage spread across the colony, electrifying the enslaved population and alarming the white planter class in equal measure. Governor Sir James Carmichael Smyth, who served as Governor of the Bahamas from 1829 to 1833 and was himself a known abolitionist, became aware of the case. He was broadly sympathetic to the plight of the enslaved and intervened decisively: the order to relocate the enslaved people to Cat Island was cancelled.

The rebellion had achieved its central goal.

Punishment and Dignity

Victory, however, came at a personal cost for Pompey. As the acknowledged leader of the rebellion, he was singled out for punishment by the plantation authorities. He was sentenced to receive 39 lashes — the maximum legally permitted flogging under colonial law.

By all historical accounts, Pompey accepted this punishment without breaking, reportedly submitting to the flogging in order to spare his fellow rebels from further retribution. His stoic endurance of this brutal public punishment only deepened his legend among the Exumian community. He had sailed across open water to challenge the most powerful institution in the colonial Caribbean, had forced a reversal of a planter's order, and had stood tall under the lash — all without surrender.

In the aftermath of the whipping, the enslaved workers on the Rolle plantation staged further unrest. They refused to work — a powerful economic weapon in a system entirely dependent on their labor — and the colonial authorities were forced to deploy military troops to restore order on the estate. The rebellion's reverberations continued long after Pompey's punishment, making clear to the colonial government that the enslaved population of the Bahamas was not passive, not compliant, and not prepared to be treated as mere property.

Governor Carmichael Smyth went further: he suspended the local colonial officials — including magistrates — who had overseen the flogging of the returning rebels, citing their excessive cruelty. This intervention caused a furious political backlash from the pro-slavery establishment in Nassau, but it also demonstrated that the moral tide was turning.

The Legacy of the Rolle Name

One of the most enduring and remarkable legacies of the Rolle plantation in Exuma is the prevalence of the surname Rolle throughout the Bahamian islands today. When slavery was formally abolished across the British Empire — first by the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 (which took effect in 1834), and then fully upon the conclusion of the Apprenticeship period in 1838 — the formerly enslaved people of Exuma faced the question of identity: who were they, now that the shackles of the law had been lifted?

Many chose, or were compelled by social convention, to adopt the surname of their former enslaver, as was common across the Caribbean. But in Exuma, this practice took on a particular power and twist. Lord John Rolle, who died in 1842 leaving no direct heirs, reportedly bequeathed his Exuma landholdings to the formerly enslaved people who had worked his estates — a remarkable act, whether motivated by guilt, pragmatism, or genuine benevolence.

As a result, the people of Exuma became landowners, community builders, and shapers of their own future. They established thriving settlements throughout Great Exuma. And they carried the surname Rolle — not as a badge of servitude, but as a marker of belonging, of community, of the land they had labored to build and had finally been allowed to own. Today, Rolle is among the most common surnames in the Bahamas, especially in Exuma, where communities like Rolleville and Rolle Town stand as testaments to the people who transformed a name of bondage into a name of pride.

Pompey, the blacksmith from Steventon, is the most celebrated of those who bore — or resisted the bearing of — that name.

Emancipation and Its Aftermath

Pompey did not live to see full emancipation come to the Bahamas. The exact date of his death is unrecorded — another casualty of a system that refused to count the humanity of enslaved people. What is certain is that his rebellion in 1830 is widely considered the pivotal act of resistance that accelerated abolitionist sentiment within the colonial administration and demonstrated to the British imperial government that the system of slavery in the Bahamas was reaching a point of unsustainability.

Four years after Pompey's rebellion, the Slavery Abolition Act brought formal emancipation to the British Empire. In the Bahamas, as elsewhere, enslaved people entered a period of Apprenticeship — a cruelly misnamed transitional arrangement that kept them bound to plantation labor for a further four years. Full, unconditional freedom came to the Bahamas in 1838.

The Bahamas that emerged from emancipation was one fundamentally shaped by the acts of resistance — large and small, dramatic and quiet — that Pompey and countless unnamed others had performed across the decades of bondage. Their insistence on being treated as human beings, their strategic use of legal channels, their willingness to absorb punishment rather than capitulate — all of this created the moral and social conditions in which emancipation became not just politically necessary, but morally inevitable.

A Hero Remembered: Monuments, Museums, and Marathons

For generations after his death, Pompey's story was preserved primarily through oral tradition — passed from grandmother to grandchild, from elder to youth, in the communities of Great Exuma. His name carried weight even when it was not written in books.

In time, formal recognition followed.

The Pompey Museum of Slavery and Emancipation, located in downtown Nassau on Bay Street and housed in the historic Vendue House — itself a former slave market where human beings were bought and sold — was dedicated in 1992 as a permanent institution preserving the history of slavery and freedom in The Bahamas. The irony and power of situating a museum honoring an enslaved freedom fighter inside a building that once auctioned enslaved people is deliberate and profound. The museum houses shackles, chains, historical documents, artifacts, and exhibits tracing the arc from the transatlantic slave trade to emancipation, with Pompey's story at its moral center.

In Steventon, Great Exuma, a memorial statue honoring Pompey stands on a seaside cliff overlooking the waters from which he launched his audacious voyage. Nearby are the ruins of the old Steventon jail, where he was held following his capture — a haunting, tangible remnant of the colonial machinery he dared to challenge.

The Run for Pompey — an annual charitable race held in Great Exuma — draws participants from across the Bahamas and beyond to run in his honor. Now in its eleventh year as of 2025, the event raises funds for the Pompey Scholarship, which provides financial support for a deserving student from Exuma to attend college or university, transforming the memory of a man denied his own freedom into opportunity for the next generation.

Most significantly, in October 2025, on National Heroes Day, Pompey was formally designated a National Hero of the Commonwealth of the Bahamas — the highest honor the nation can bestow. He joined a select pantheon of figures who shaped Bahamian identity, including Hubert Ingraham and other foundational leaders of the modern Bahamian state. For the people of Exuma — many of them descendants of the very community Pompey fought to protect — this recognition was long overdue and deeply personal.

"Pompey's rebellion was not merely a moment of individual courage. It was a collective declaration by an entire community that they were human beings who could not be moved, displaced, or destroyed without a fight."

The Enduring Meaning of Pompey

What makes Pompey's story so extraordinary — and so relevant — is not just the dramatic events of 1830, but the strategic intelligence and moral clarity he brought to an impossible situation. He did not simply flee. He did not simply endure. He organized, he planned, he sailed across open water, and he petitioned the highest authority available to him. He used the systems of empire against the slaveholders of empire, and he won — at the cost of 39 lashes across his back.

His rebellion reminds us that resistance to injustice does not always look like violence. Sometimes it looks like 44 people slipping into the bush at night, seizing a boat at dawn, and sailing toward justice across 130 miles of open Caribbean sea.

For generations of Bahamians — and particularly for the people of Exuma, who carry in their very surnames the complex, painful, and resilient history of the Rolle plantations — Pompey is not merely a historical figure. He is an ancestor, a protector, a proof that dignity and courage could survive even the most brutal conditions human beings have ever inflicted upon one another.

The communities that grew from the ashes of the Rolle plantation — Steventon, Rolleville, Rolle Town, and beyond — and the children of Exuma who today receive scholarships in his name, are the living legacy of a 32-year-old blacksmith who, one day in 1830, decided that enough was enough.

L.W. Young, among other Bahamian educators and historians, has worked to ensure that stories like Pompey's are passed on to future generations — recognizing that national identity, for the Bahamas, is inseparable from the memory of those who fought for freedom in the darkest hours of the colonial era.

Pompey of Exuma belongs not only to the history of The Bahamas, but to the universal history of human dignity and resistance.

Major Contributions

  • Pompey's most significant contribution to Bahamian and Caribbean history was his leadership of the 1830 Exuma rebellion — the first major organized act of collective resistance against slavery in the Bahamas — which directly resulted in the cancellation of Lord John Rolle's order to forcibly relocate 77 enslaved people from Steventon, Exuma, to Cat Island.
  • By organizing and executing a bold, non-violent strategy of refusal, flight, and direct petition to colonial authorities, Pompey demonstrated that enslaved people could use the mechanisms of imperial governance as a tool of their own protection, and that their collective action could force concrete reversals of planter decisions.
  • His rebellion drew the attention of Governor James Carmichael Smyth, whose intervention — and subsequent suspension of the officials who brutalized the rebels — shifted the political landscape of the colony and accelerated the movement toward emancipation four years later.
  • Beyond the immediate events of 1830, Pompey's enduring contribution is symbolic and cultural: he has become the defining icon of Bahamian resistance to slavery, honored by the Pompey Museum of Slavery and Emancipation in Nassau (housed in the former Vendue House slave market), a memorial statue in Steventon, the annual Run for Pompey charitable race and scholarship in Exuma, and his formal designation as a National Hero of the Commonwealth of the Bahamas in October 2025.
  • His story preserves the memory of all the unnamed enslaved people who built the Bahamian nation, and his legacy continues to inspire new generations through education, commemoration, and the ongoing work of cultural memory.
